Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · School & learning

derive verb

of a word or a name: come from, be formed from

also be derived from, derivation, come from (of a word), be named after, take its name from

classical

Cic. Fin. 5.18: ab aliquā rē tōtīus vītae dūcere exōrdium (Lewis & Short)
Quint. 1.6.3: nōmen ā Graecō (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. etymology: orīginem dūcere (vel trahere)

dūcō, dūcere, dūxī, ductum

verb, third conjugation: nōmen, orīginem dūcere ab (or ex) with the ablative

draw, derive (a name, a beginning) from

Lewis & Short: “to draw, deduce, derive its origin or beginning from”. The first sense is “lead”; ductus has a short u (the voiceless stop before it blocks Lachmann’s law).

Other words

  • trahō, trahere, trāxī, tractum — get, take (a name) from

    verb, third conjugation, with ex or ab and the ablative · also used · classical · Cic. Phil. 3.16: quī cognōmen ex contumēliā trāxerit (Lewis & Short); Ov. M. 4.291: nōmen ab illīs (Lewis & Short)

  • dīcī ab — be called after, be so named from

    phrase: passive of dīcō, with ab and the ablative, or ab eō quod with a clause · also used · classical · Varr. LL 5.21: terra dicta ab eō … quod teritur

    The grammarians’ way of giving an etymology, true or false: Varro’s is a folk etymology.

  • dērīvō, dērīvāre, dērīvāvī, dērīvātum — derive (one word from another)

    verb, first conjugation, with ab and the ablative · also used · post-classical · Quint. 1.6.38 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 246, 303: dērīvāre (ab); Traupman 294

    Lewis & Short: in this sense post-Augustan, “for dūcere”. Classically it means to lead off water from a river (Caes. B.G. 7.72), and so to divert (blame, anger) onto someone.

Examples

  • quī cognōmen ex contumēliā trāxerit

    a man who got his surname from an insultCic. Phil. 3.16 (Lewis & Short)

  • terra dicta ab eō, ut Aelius scrībit, quod teritur

    terra (earth) is so called, as Aelius writes, because it is trodden (a folk etymology)Varr. LL 5.21

See also derive, source, word.
